newsitem.title: USA: Tentative pact reached in McDonnell Douglas strike.
newsitem.headline: Tentative pact reached in McDonnell Douglas strike.

text.p: McDonnell Douglas Corp. reached tentative agreement Friday with the International Association of Machinists to end a 94-day strike by 6,700 workers in St. Louis, House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt announced.

"As a member of the St. Louis community, I am pleased to announce that a tentative agreement has been reached, pending ratification of the membership, to bring an end to the dispute between the machinists union and the McDonnell Douglas Corp.," said Gephardt at news conference, flanked by union and company representatives.
The strike revolved around the issue of job security, with union members concerned their jobs would evaporate by being subcontracted to companies in distant cities.
Labour Secretary Robert Reich congratulated labour and management for reaching the agreement.

"This tenative agreement shows that even in an era of economic transition, labour and management can resolve tough issues like job security if they are willing to work together," he said in a statement.
"This strike has strained our economy and put many of our families at risk," Gephardt told reporters, adding that the deal meant that jobs would remain in St. Louis.

"I believe that as a result of this agreement McDonnell Douglas will be a more successful competitor," he said. "I think jobs can be kept in St. Louis and I think everybody can win from this solution."

The agreement is tentative, however, pending approval by union members. Gerry Oulson, president of District 837 of the union, said he hoped a ratification meeting could be arranged by Wednesday or Thursday. Until then, all sides declined to discuss terms of the agreement.
Strike talks were conducted in St. Louis until they broke down on Aug. 16 when union leaders said the company was unwilling to discuss job security.
Late in August, Gephardt invited them back to the table in his Washington office. Thousands of machinists and other McDonnell Douglas employees live in Gephardt's district.
Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service Director John Calhoun Wells said the final agreement was reached in 30 hours of non-stop bargaining with federal mediators.
Analyst Kent Newcomb of A.G. Edwards & Sons said settlement of the three-month-old McDonnell Douglas strike removed an element of uncertainty.
"Investors would rather have their company not be on strike," he noted, "assuming they (management) did not give away the store."
"There will probably need to be some fence mending, but overall it was not a terribly vicious strike," Newcomb added.
